title: Pope Leo XIV Celebrates Massive Open-Air Mass in Paris
summary:
An estimated 700,000 people filled the Place de la Concorde in Paris on Saturday for an open-air Mass led by Pope Leo XIV. The pontiff arrived in his open-topped popemobile, waving to crowds as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue.

During the Mass, the Pope praised the "enthusiasm, energy and commitment" young people bring to the Catholic Church. He called them "today's Church" and told worshippers not to keep their faith private. "Let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed," he said.

The visit is a four-day trip to France. On Friday, the Pope met President Emmanuel Macron and joined 80,000 young people at the Stade de France. Macron did not attend Saturday's Mass — France has strict rules on the separation of church and state. But his wife Brigitte Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu were there, along with several presidential candidates.

Earlier Saturday, the Pope visited the Maison Bakhita centre, which supports refugees. He praised the organization for inviting people "to see those who are invisible" and stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love." He also warned about the dangers of artificial intelligence.

The Church believes the large crowds reflect growing spirituality in France and Europe. More events are planned for the rest of the Pope's visit.
why_it_matters: The visit shows how a religious leader can draw enormous crowds in a country that legally separates religion from government — and how the Church is trying to speak to young people about faith, refugees and new technology.

background_read: Pope Leo XIV (the head of the Roman Catholic Church worldwide) made a four-day visit to France — a country with a deep Catholic history but also a strong tradition of keeping religion out of government.

That tradition is called laïcité, and it goes back to a 1905 law that separated church and state. It is why President Emmanuel Macron (France's president since 2017) stayed away from the Mass, while his wife Brigitte Macron and Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu attended.

The Place de la Concorde, where the Mass was held, is one of Paris's biggest public squares, sitting at the end of the Champs-Élysées, the famous avenue the popemobile drove down. The Stade de France, north of Paris, is the national stadium, built for the 1998 football World Cup.
The Maison Bakhita is named after Josephine Bakhita, a woman born in Sudan who was enslaved as a child and later became a Catholic saint; the centre now supports refugees in the Paris area.

perspectives.description: The Vatican and French Catholics read the 700,000-strong crowd as evidence of growing spirituality in France and Europe, where church attendance has fallen for decades. The Pope's focus on young people as 'today's Church' is meant to show that faith is alive and public, not private. Organisers say the rest of the visit will build on that momentum.

Supporters of France's strict separation of church and state argue that a papal visit of this scale sits awkwardly in a country that deliberately keeps religion out of public power. They see Macron's absence as the correct, legally required signal, even while his wife and prime minister attended. From this angle, the state should be careful not to look like it is endorsing one religion.

Big papal events are usually built around chosen themes, and this one pushed refugees, the role of women in the Church, and the risks of artificial intelligence. Those themes travel through the crowd and the media far beyond the churchgoers present. At the same time, the Church faces long-term pressures such as falling numbers of priests and worshippers in Europe.

The open question is whether enthusiasm at a Mass turns into lasting participation in Church life, especially among the young people the Pope addressed. France must also keep managing very large religious gatherings inside a secular legal framework. How the remaining days of the visit unfold will show which message sticks.
